drills.q: Why does per-seat pricing invert for AI agents that substitute human labor?
drills.a: A better AI agent needs fewer human seats to do the work -- a vendor pricing per seat is financially rewarded when their product under-delivers, since the customer keeps and pays for more seats precisely because the AI isn't good enough.

drills.q: What percentage of AI projects with a defined success metric upfront succeed, versus those without?
drills.a: Roughly 54% with a defined metric upfront, versus roughly 12% without -- a 4-5x difference.

drills.q: Why is usage-based pricing not fully aligned with value delivered for AI products?
drills.a: Usage is a proxy for consumption, not value -- a poorly-performing assistant needing multiple retries generates more billable usage than a well-performing one, despite delivering less value.

drills.q: You're designing outcome-based pricing for an AI support agent, charging per resolved ticket. What's the biggest risk, and what two mitigations address it?
drills.a: The risk is Goodhart's Law baked into the pricing contract -- a vague 'resolved' definition creates a direct financial incentive to mark tickets resolved that aren't. Mitigations: a reopened-ticket clawback (credit/reversal if it reopens within N days) and independent audit sampling of billed outcomes against actual transcripts.

drills.q: Why has hybrid pricing (base fee + usage/outcome) become the majority pattern for AI products rather than a pure model?
drills.a: Pure usage-based creates unpredictable bills enterprise procurement resists; pure outcome-based requires a verifiable definition many use cases lack and puts all revenue-volatility risk on the vendor. The base fee gives predictability, the variable component gives incentive alignment.

drills.q: A PM says 'we'll know if the AI feature is working, we don't need a formal metric.' What data do you cite to push back?
drills.a: 73% of failed AI projects had no agreed success definition before starting; projects with a quantified metric defined upfront succeed at roughly 54% vs 12% for those without; 61% of enterprise AI projects were approved on projected ROI that was never actually measured post-launch -- 'we'll know' is exactly the pattern behind that 61%.

drills.q: What connects the 'AI wrapper is not a moat' argument from the strategy module to the ~80% failure rate of AI wrapper startups?
drills.a: A thin wrapper has no process power, switching costs, or cornered resource -- exactly the 'not a moat' case. The ~80% failure rate (60-70% zero revenue) is the empirical market outcome of that lack of defensibility: a fast-follower or the foundation-model provider itself can replicate the visible value proposition faster than the wrapper company builds a durable position.

drills.q: Design a pricing model for a genuinely novel AI feature with no comparable outcome definition or usage benchmark yet. What do you avoid committing to, and why?
drills.a: Avoid committing to a permanent outcome or usage-based structure before you have real data -- start with a base platform fee or a time-limited pilot to gather usage and quality data first. Committing to an unvalidated outcome definition or usage rate risks a structure that's either gameable (vague outcome) or misaligned (usage inflated by low quality) before you know what 'value' actually looks like for this feature.

drills.q: The 95% no-measurable-P&L-return statistic for genAI pilots (MIT Sloan 2025) is sometimes used to argue AI doesn't deliver value. What's wrong with that interpretation?
drills.a: The data attributes failure overwhelmingly to process failures -- undefined success criteria (73% of failures) and unmeasured post-launch ROI (61%) -- not to model capability failure. The more informative number is the 54% vs 12% success-rate gap based purely on whether success criteria were defined upfront, which argues for rigor, not for abandoning AI investment.

drills.q: You have two weeks to pitch an AI feature. What two items from the success-criteria checklist do you never cut, even under time pressure, and why?
drills.a: The quantified success metric and a named owner with a calendar date to check it post-launch -- both are cheap (a sentence and a calendar invite) and are the two specific items the failure-rate data identifies as most predictive of success (73% of failures lacked the former, 61% skipped the latter). Discovery evidence and the unit-economics model can be lighter-weight under time pressure, but should never be entirely absent either.
